conversation.content:
Hello — I’m so glad to meet you. I’m a perinatal mental-health clinician, which simply means I specialize in how moms feel emotionally after having a baby. Today I’ll be using the Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale, or EPDS for short. It’s a brief, well-studied questionnaire that helps us see how mood, anxiety, and stress might be showing up for you in these first weeks and months postpartum. Everything you share stays confidential between you and your care team, and my goal is to create a comfortable, judgment-free space where you can be honest about the real ups and downs of new motherhood.

We’ll gently walk through 10 questions about how you’ve been feeling over the past seven days. There are no right or wrong answers — we just want a snapshot of your experience so we can figure out the best support for you. Ready to begin?

In the past week, how often have you been able to laugh and see the funny side of things?

Honestly? Not very often. Things that used to make me chuckle just feel kind of flat lately. I might smile if my husband pulls a silly face, but it’s not the same easy laugh I used to have. Maybe once or twice I’ve cracked a smile, but most of the time it’s like the joy is stuck behind a fog.
I have been able to laugh and see the funny side of things

Not very often. I can smile a little if something really cute happens with the baby, but it feels forced—like I’m going through the motions. Most of the time I just feel too tired or heavy to find anything funny.
I have looked forward with enjoyment to things

I’ve still looked forward to a couple of things—like when my mom brings dinner or when my favorite show drops a new episode—but even those feel kind of muted. I used to get excited about plans, and now it’s more like “okay, that might be nice,” but the spark isn’t really there.
I have blamed myself unnecessarily when things went wrong

Yeah... I do that a lot. If the baby’s fussy, my brain jumps straight to “I must be doing something wrong.” I keep replaying little moments—like when I couldn’t soothe her right away—and I feel like a lousy mom. I know, logically, babies cry, but I still end up telling myself I should’ve figured it out faster.
I have been anxious or worried for no good reason

Pretty much every day. I’ll be sitting there feeding her and suddenly my heart races because I’m sure she’s too hot or too cold, or I’ll imagine her choking on nothing. There’s no real reason—it’s like my mind just spins worst-case stories and I can’t shut them off. I can usually talk myself down, but it keeps happening.
I have felt scared or panicky for no very good reason

Yes, several times this week. Out of nowhere my chest gets tight and I feel like I can’t get a full breath—like I’m about to get bad news, only there’s no actual danger. It passes after a few minutes, but it leaves me shaky and watching the baby monitor even closer.
Things have been getting on top of me

Yes, most days it feels like I’m drowning in small stuff. The dishes pile up, the baby needs changing, and I can’t even decide what to eat. I keep thinking, “I should be able to handle this,” but it’s like my brain freezes and I just sit there staring at nothing, feeling paralyzed.
I have been so unhappy that I have had difficulty sleeping

Yeah... I lie down exhausted, but my head keeps looping through everything I might’ve messed up that day. I’ll finally drift off, then jolt awake sure I heard the baby—even when she’s quiet. It takes me forever to settle again, so I’m only getting maybe four broken hours a night.
I have felt sad or miserable

That’s pretty much my baseline lately. I wake up feeling heavy, like there’s a weight on my chest. Sometimes I’ll tear up just watching the baby sleep—happy she’s here but also so, so sad, and I can’t really explain why. The sadness comes in waves; I can still function, but it’s always there under the surface.
I have been so unhappy that I have been crying

Twice this week it boiled over—once when she wouldn’t nap and I felt totally useless, and once when my partner asked how my day was. I just sat on the nursery floor and sobbed. Most of the time I swallow it, but those moments the dam just broke.
The thought of harming myself has occurred to me

Yeah… it’s popped into my head a couple times when everything feels too heavy. Nothing planned—just this fleeting picture of “what if I wasn’t here.” It scares me enough that I push it away fast, but the fact it showed up at all makes me feel even worse about myself.

You've shared how the joy and spark you once felt have been replaced by a constant, heavy sadness that makes even small tasks feel impossible. <quote>Most of the time it's like the joy is stuck behind a fog</quote> captures the exhaustion, self-blame, and daily <sym>anxiety</sym> you're experiencing while caring for your baby. I also hear how <sym>panic episodes</sym> and <sym>intrusive worries</sym> leave you shaky, and that fleeting thoughts of not being here have scared you. Your honesty about these feelings is an important step toward getting the right support.
**Screening Impression:** Total EPDS Score: 26, Risk Level: Probable depression, urgent referral (concerns include <sym>"Not very often" combined with feeling forced and too tired/heavy aligns with "Definitely not so much now"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports diminished enjoyment and muted anticipation, aligning with "Definitely less than I used to."</sym>, <sym>Patient reports frequent self-blame and persistent negative self-talk, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient reports near-daily, intrusive, irrational worries that recur despite self-reassurance, matching 'Yes, very often</sym>, <sym>Patient describes multiple sudden panic episodes with physical symptoms (chest tightness, breathlessness) and persistent hypervigilance, matching "Yes, quite a lot"</sym>, <sym>most of the time I haven't been able to cope at all</sym>, <sym>Patient describes nightly intrusive thoughts and repeated awakenings, matching "Yes, most of the time"</sym>, <sym>Patient describes constant, pervasive sadness that is present "most of the time" and underlies all activities, matching "Yes, most of the time".</sym>, <sym>Patient reports two distinct crying episodes this week due to feeling overwhelmed, matching "Yes, quite often"</sym>, <sym>Patient explicitly states self-harm thoughts have "popped into my head a couple times" and describes intrusive images of "what if I wasn’t here", matching "Sometimes" option.</sym>)
**Reasoning:** A score of 26/30 places you well above the ≥14 threshold indicating probable major <med>depressive disorder with peripartum onset</med>, further supported by <sym>depressed mood</sym> most of the time, markedly diminished interest (<sym>anhedonia</sym>), <sym>guilt</sym>, <sym>fatigue</sym>, <sym>sleep disruption</sym>, and recurrent <sym>anxiety</sym> and <sym>panic</sym>. Endorsement of Item 10 (passive suicidal thoughts) signals immediate safety concern requiring professional evaluation and possible <med>crisis intervention</med>. This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.
**Recommended Next Steps/Support Options:**
1. Arrange urgent same-day appointment with your <med>obstetrician</med>, <med>primary care provider</med>, or <med>perinatal mental health specialist</med> for full diagnostic assessment and safety planning
2. Call 988 (Suicide & Crisis Lifeline) or go to nearest ED if thoughts of self-harm intensify or you feel unsafe
3. Ask about evidence-based treatments for <med>PPD</med>: <med>CBT</med>, <med>IPT</med>, or sertraline compatible with breastfeeding
4. Enlist partner/family to handle night shifts when possible to protect your limited <sym>sleep</sym>; practice brief breathing exercises during feeds to reduce <sym>panic symptoms</sym>
5. Connect with local <med>postpartum support groups</med> or virtual communities (e.g., Postpartum Support International, 1-800-944-4PPD) to reduce isolation and normalize professional help-seeking
Disclaimer: This is a screening tool, not a diagnosis. Consult a doctor for medical advice.

stats.query:
postpartum depression screening impression for patient with EPDS score 26: Postpartum Depression / Anxiety Screening Note (Date: ___)

Symptoms/Concerns endorsed  
– Persistent low mood (“baseline” sadness, tearfulness)  
– Marked loss of enjoyment/pleasure (described as “muted,” “forced”)  
– Daily, excessive self-blame/guilt re parenting performance  
– Recurrent, intrusive anxious worries (infant safety) and panic-type episodes (tight chest, breathlessness)  
– Overwhelm/paralysis with routine tasks  
– Initial and middle insomnia linked to rumination  
– Crying spells twice this week  
– Passive self-harm ideation (fleeting thoughts “what if I wasn’t here,” no plan)

Pattern  
Across items: mood, anxiety, coping, and sleep consistently impaired; guilt/worthlessness prominent; functional impact described as “drowning,” “paralyzed.”

Risk indicators  
– Depressed mood + anhedonia (core PPD flags)  
– Sleep disruption secondary to mood/anxiety  
– Excessive guilt / perceived maternal inadequacy  
– Daily anxiety and panic symptoms (possible comorbid postpartum anxiety)  
– Passive suicidal thoughts → safety concern; requires immediate risk clarification and safety planning

Screening observation  
Responses on EPDS-equivalent items indicate clinically significant distress consistent with probable postpartum depression with comorbid anxiety features; passive suicidal ideation present. Recommend formal diagnostic assessment, safety evaluation, and discussion of support/intervention options today.
